title: Tiara Time and Data Center Politics: Vanderbilt’s AI Governance Playbook with Cat Moon and Mark Williams
author: Cat Moon · Mark Williams

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source discusses a broad, full-stack approach to understanding and teaching AI but provides no substantive view on whether automation threatens associate expertise reproduction or how legal apprenticeship should be reconstructed. The only relevant material consists of unanswered host questions about legal education and technology integration.
qs: How are law schools going to prepare students for the transition to practice?
Is there going to be more blended technology?

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source describes an infrastructure-oriented approach to teaching AI and raises questions about technology’s role in preparing law students for practice. It does not address whether automation weakens apprenticeship or partner succession, nor does it evaluate the cluster’s proposed responses such as funded development, simulation, feedback or broader career paths.
qs: How are law schools going to prepare students for the transition to practice?
Is there going to be more blended technology?

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source’s aspiration for more direct discussion in legal education loosely relates to organisational preparation, but the excerpt does not specify AI governance, human control, implementation, pricing or employment. Its prediction that labs will proliferate is unsupported and does not establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: And I hope that we’re forcing those discussions in a more direct way throughout the way we educate our law students, I would say.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source accepts selective, practical continuous learning and materially develops it through mission-aligned student tool building, outside-law monitoring and full-stack AI education. Its acknowledgment of excessive AI consumption also reinforces the need for filtering, though its claims remain experiential rather than outcome-based.
qs: And so something like that, we feel comfortable kind of getting our hands around and using its primary a learning vehicle.
⁓ But it’s, ⁓ it’s all, yeah, I probably have too many things that I’m consuming because it’s, ⁓ as they say with, with models, you know, you can overfit to your training dad.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: The source accepts that technological and structural change is disrupting junior apprenticeship and requiring legal-training reform. It materially extends the proposition by advocating joint redesign among educators, practitioners and students rather than shifting responsibility to either schools or employers alone, while presenting this as an aspiration rather than a validated model.
qs: The thing that’s interesting to me is whether it’s taking place outside of law school that directly impacts it is that we are messing with that guild model of knowledge work and we are taking away a lot of those ⁓ foundational sort of bricklaying skills that used to be done by first and second year associates that’s increasingly getting commoditized and being shrunk down to zero.

And as legal education is figuring out what are we best prepared and suited to provide and what do we need to change, there’s so much room in the middle, right, for the stakeholders and I would also say students.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that embedded legal AI requires selective, human-led use rather than assumptions of general competence. It materially extends that proposition with concrete implementation priorities: experiential legal education, interdisciplinary governance, definable procurement standards, and capacity-sensitive deployment, especially for smaller firms.
qs: ⁓ But we’re rather using it as an assistant throughout the learning process, but not as the final result.

Mark Williams (34:03)  ⁓ cause so much of what you’re just talking about right there is just procurement, And coming up with, ⁓ definable standards about what, what it means to procure AI systems in this, which is really getting back to a data question.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s shift from AI availability and use toward the organisational work required for responsible deployment. It specifically foregrounds internal management, regulation and compliance, but does not substantively address workflow value, renewal economics, consumption costs or platform control, and offers questions rather than findings or a concrete governance framework.
qs: It’s like, well, what does it mean to responsibly deploy this to manage it within an organization?

kp.k: AI governance requires interdisciplinary coordination and shared definitions
kp.d: Williams describes Vanderbilt’s inaugural symposium as a response to divergent meanings of governance, spanning responsible deployment, organizational ownership, compliance and regulation. Discussions included law-firm frameworks, corporate boards and legal teams, and collaboration between law and computer science students. He reports that several research projects emerged from informal exchanges, with further coursework and another symposium planned; these are institutional observations rather than evaluated outcomes.
qs: everybody means something different when they say governance, honestly.
we had sessions on thinking about building compliance and governance frameworks within a law firm, but also if you’re in-house at a large corporation
several research projects had sort of bounced out of those sessions

kp.k: Data centers connect AI governance with energy politics
kp.d: Williams reports that energy use moved from a niche policy topic in late spring and early summer to a salient public issue by the symposium, asserting that local elections were being decided around pro- and anti-data-center positions. His expectation that the issue will affect forthcoming midterms is predictive. Lambert separately reports discussions in an energy practice group about Texas data centers, energy access and prospective on-site generation.
qs: local elections were being decided by candidates running as either I’m the AI, I’m the anti data center candidate or I’m the pro data center candidate.
This will be a topic of discussion.
A lot of these data centers are thinking that they’re just going to  self-sufficient in their energy. They’re going to build on site.

kp.k: AI training extends beyond research into business development
kp.d: Discussing training materials he reviews, Williams argues that legal AI education should move beyond one-shot chat and legal research toward competitive intelligence and business development using financial and business data. He characterizes these as useful applications that students may not previously have encountered, not as measured productivity findings.
qs: moving beyond just chat one shot
bolted on to good like financial services and business data resources.
It’s you don’t just have to use this to search Westlaw. It’s way more dynamic than that.

kp.k: Student exposure grows while platform integration reduces optionality
kp.d: Williams reports that, over the preceding two years, returning students increasingly described formal summer AI training and experience with, or questions about, Harvey. He stresses uneven preparedness and firms’ continuing uncertainty about use cases. He also characterizes generative AI’s integration into research platforms as making its use less of a separate, optional decision.
qs: Like I’ve never experienced.  students come back and ask about a specific legal tool like they did this summer
My sense is that they come back is that the firms were still figuring out what exactly they were supposed to be doing with it.
it’s not this optional thing. It’s now just infused in everything.

kp.k: Clear course policies matter more than blanket AI anxiety
kp.d: Moon observes broader but uneven adoption in legal education, often still as peripheral training rather than a consistent institutional approach. She recommends clear course-specific rules to give students confidence, while opposing mandatory integration in every course. Lambert reports encountering students deterred by perceived ethics restrictions; Moon argues that framing use primarily as an honor-code threat is unhelpful.
qs: My observation is that legal education is continuing its embrace of generative AI in that same way for the most part.
what I hear consistently from my students is they just want guidance in a particular course
This isn’t mandatory. I don’t think it should be mandatory.
students arriving, like I don’t want to touch it because at my school that’s an honor code violation. And I don’t think that’s helpful.

kp.k: Gender adoption concerns motivate participatory AI literacy initiatives
kp.d: Moon distinguishes reports of slower AI uptake among women from stronger predictions of widening employment and pay gaps. She acknowledges suggestive studies but questions the solidity of evidence for an epidemic; no study identifiers or samples are supplied. Her response is a cross-disciplinary, women-focused but inclusive initiative emphasizing co-created content, AI literacy, practical workshop outputs and collaboration rather than discussion alone.
qs: there are data ⁓ to suggest that uptake by women has been slower.
I don’t believe the data is super solid that this is like an epidemic.
it is not for women only.
The  objective is that everyone walks out of a workshop with some kind of actionable artifact
the entire theme of the Women in AI Summit 2.0 is AI literacy.

kp.k: Smaller firms need procurement frameworks under resource constraints
kp.d: Drawing primarily on work with boutique and mid-sized firms, Williams identifies limited budgets, scarce procurement expertise and excessive vendor choice as central barriers. He recommends frameworks that narrow options according to use cases, organizational comfort, available resources and expected returns, rather than prescribing one product. He reports a shift from curiosity about AI toward questions about production deployment, while retaining a research-and-development qualification.
qs: They’re overwhelmed by choice. They have a limited amount of resources. They have one shot at this to buy maybe one thing.
We have a limited amount of budget. We have a limited amount of time to get buy-in.
How do we take it from out of novelty and into production? Now it’s still a research and development process.

kp.k: Governance standards provide an emerging floor, not complete assurance
kp.d: Williams reports improvement in vendor agreement language and emerging firm adoption of ISO 42001. He presents certification as shorthand for management maturity, but only a baseline. He argues that many public and private standards originated around narrower AI systems, describing general-purpose generative AI as complicating the EU AI Act’s development. Questions about high-risk deployment, legal decision-making and unauthorized practice remain unresolved in his account; he reports some maturation over the preceding eight to 12 months rather than offering legal conclusions.
qs: there’s just now sort of firms starting to adopt like ISO 42001
it’s a good floor
they’re really geared towards an older, mature version of machine learning and narrower deterministic AI systems.
What is a legal service? And so it goes into sort of UPL and all these definitions that we never had any agreement on to begin with.
I think just now over the last eight to 12 months, you’re starting to see a little bit of maturity

kp.k: Rapid feature changes undermine one-time procurement security reviews
kp.d: Lambert identifies changes within already approved products as a major operational problem, citing external collaboration features in Legora and Harvey that were not covered by earlier security review and may arrive without timely awareness. Williams adds that Harvey’s internet-searching deep research capability changes the closed-universe premise on which some tools were purchased. These are practitioner concerns about changing deployment boundaries, not reports of demonstrated breaches.
qs: the biggest issue we have, not just with information security data governance, is the advancements in the tools that we already have that have already passed all of these security requirements.
now the big thing with like Legora and Harvey is this external collaboration with clients and others. Well, that was not something that cleared the security muster
sometimes we don’t even know it’s being introduced
the whole reason you bought them is because they were a closed universe and kept them in house. And that’s what you contracted for.

kp.k: Client requirements shape tool choice and slow deployment
kp.d: Gebauer identifies information literacy and complex outside-counsel guidelines and engagement letters as post-procurement barriers: permissions may require repeated checking, conversations and possibly consent. Williams reports practitioners describing large institutional clients that dictate which AI tool outside firms must use. Moon treats this as an extension of longstanding client platform requirements, rather than an entirely new source of buyer power.
qs: the complexity and broadness of requirements and like outside council guidelines and engagement letters. That is a huge challenge
Maybe consent has to happen each time.
larger institutional clients come in with their own sort of AI preferences.
we will work with this tool. If you would like to continue, like this is where we will be operating.
think clients have been doing that forever.

kp.k: AI literacy must distinguish capabilities from marketing labels
kp.d: Williams reports that a previously elaborate quiz-generation prompt has become a simple interface button, illustrating how training can become outdated. He also questions loose uses of the term agent, recounting a firm user’s comparison of a Copilot feature to a macro. He positions current literacy work as helping firms interpret capabilities and buzzwords, not merely introducing basic AI concepts.
qs: literally that prompt now is just this button that you push and it says like, make me a quiz
felt like it was just a macro to me.
a lot of the word. talk about like AI literacy.
a buzzword, right? And so dispelling some of that.

kp.k: Continuous change may demand new professional working arrangements
kp.d: Moon questions whether simply fitting AI into existing ethics rules is sufficient as integration deepens. She predicts continuing rapid change will force reconsideration of working methods and recommends greater communication, collaboration and transparency. This is a normative and forward-looking argument, not a determination that particular rules have ceased to apply.
qs: our existing ethics rules can handle this just fine, right? Let’s just point to the rules that already exist and figure out how this fits. I don’t think it’s that simple.
This isn’t going to suddenly stop or slow down.
this is going to require a lot more communication, collaboration, and transparency.

kp.k: Academic tool access enables more concrete practice preparation
kp.d: Williams contrasts early teaching, largely limited to theory and general ChatGPT access, with the preceding year’s expanded availability of legal-specific tools. He reports that students can now experiment and fail safely with tools resembling those used in firms. He attributes institutional progress to an experienced team and processes for intake, deployment, measurement and iteration, but supplies no quantified learning results.
qs: everything was kind of theory.
letting them ⁓ safely experiment with them, safely fail with them
this is the actual.  tool that you will have and the training that you will get when you are in your firm.
intake, deploy, track, measure, and iterate

kp.k: Learning labs distinguish prototyping from sustainable product delivery
kp.d: Moon explains that VAILL increasingly defines itself as a learning and teaching lab because maintaining deployed products is difficult and expensive. It partners with organizations equipped to build rather than assuming full product ownership. Williams cites a Tennessee end-of-life planning prototype as prompting questions about long-term robustness and maintenance, while defending building as interdisciplinary learning. Moon identifies an AI regulatory tracker and a planned curated learning-resource repository, 'the list,' as more closely aligned with the lab’s mission; the latter is described as under development.
qs: we are primarily a learning lab, A learning and teaching lab
it is very hard to build, deploy, and maintain something.
we partner with organizations who want to build
building as a vehicle for learning.
we built a Tennessee end of life planning tool.
it’s going to be a curated interactive, of course, GenAI powered repository for learning resources about generative AI.

kp.k: Automation challenges apprenticeship and foundational skill acquisition
kp.d: Williams argues that AI is disrupting the guild model by commoditizing foundational work traditionally done by first- and second-year associates, raising unresolved questions about how novices acquire expertise. He reports encouraging student awareness of cognitive offloading but explicitly limits that observation to self-selecting second- and third-year students in his AI course and acknowledges shortcuts may occur. His account offers concerns and classroom observations, not measured job displacement or skill-loss estimates.
qs: I have the luxury of teaching an AI class that second and third year law students choose to be in.
they’re coming at it from a self-selecting sort of mindset
being aware of cognitive offload
we are messing with that guild model of knowledge work
foundational sort of bricklaying skills that used to be done by first and second year associates that’s increasingly getting commoditized and being shrunk down to zero.
What do we do to get those students up to that level of skill?

kp.k: Ownership changes add uncertainty to future lawyer formation
kp.d: Williams identifies potential changes to law-firm ownership and business models as additional external pressures on education. He mentions discussions of alternative ownership in Tennessee, private-equity interest and emerging AI-first firms, asking how these developments affect skill building. He frames them as open questions and possible changes, not enacted ownership reforms or established market outcomes.
qs: the ownership rules, the law firm model is potentially changing.
even here in Tennessee, we’re having some discussions about, you know, alternative ownership
private equity is kind of starting to knock on the door.
AI first law firms starting to pop up. What does that mean? How does skill building play into that?

kp.k: Legal education should be co-created through continuing iteration
kp.d: Asked to predict the future, Moon explicitly offers the future she wants: collaboration among educators, firms and students rather than separate institutional demands and fixed divisions of training responsibility. She argues that uncertainty about the future human lawyer creates an opportunity to redesign preparation together, and expects iteration to become part of legal education. She does not specify a settled curriculum or claim to know firms’ future requirements.
qs: I’m gonna talk about the future I want to see.
this invites radical collaboration
what do we really need from a human lawyer going forward, right? There are a lot of unanswered questions there.
I would also say students. So often they seem kind of left out of these conversations
we are kind of entering this era of iteration that’s going to apply to legal education as well.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Williams describes legal AI adoption as increasingly embedded and students' exposure as increasingly practical, but uneven.
pts.d: At 10:58–14:47, Mark Williams reports that more returning students have received summer training, used legal-specific tools, or asked about Harvey. He distinguishes exposure from competence and says firms are still figuring out appropriate uses. He also argues that embedding generative AI in mainstream research platforms is making adoption less optional. These are observations from teaching and engagements, rather than measured adoption rates.

pts.k: Williams sees useful applications beyond legal research and expects tool interfaces to absorb some elaborate prompting work.
pts.d: At 10:58 and 41:32–42:25, Williams identifies competitive intelligence and business development, particularly with financial and business data, as useful applications. His example of quiz generation becoming a button illustrates why he no longer expects elaborate prompt engineering to develop as previously imagined. He also cautions that 'agent' has become a marketing buzzword; the discussion does not establish that all products so labelled perform autonomous multi-step work.

pts.k: Moon says legal education is embracing AI mainly at the margins, while clear course guidance improves student confidence and competence.
pts.d: At 16:34–19:24, Cat Moon describes adoption across legal education as uneven and usually an add-on rather than a consistently integrated approach. She acknowledges some mandatory introductory training. Her inference that coherent policies remain uncommon is expressly qualified by what institutions are publicly discussing. She favours clear rules without requiring every professor to integrate AI, and regards blanket honour-code fears as unhelpful.

pts.k: Williams says smaller firms need procurement decision frameworks as AI moves from novelty toward production.
pts.d: At 34:03–43:23, Williams describes boutique and mid-sized firms as facing many products, limited budgets, limited implementation time, and insufficient dedicated procurement expertise. Their questions increasingly concern actionable selection and return on investment rather than whether AI matters. He contrasts these firms with larger firms that more often possess established processes, while still characterising deployment as early-stage research and development.

pts.k: Williams describes maturing AI procurement standards alongside unresolved legal definitions and frameworks originally oriented toward narrower AI.
pts.d: At 35:00–39:10, Williams reports improvement in vendor agreements and emerging use of ISO 42001 as a baseline signal of AI-management maturity, not a complete assurance. He says many public and private frameworks were oriented toward narrower machine-learning systems. His discussion of legal decision-making, legal services and unauthorized practice raises conditional interpretive questions, not a finding that a particular deployment violates a law.

pts.k: Williams says new features can change the operational boundaries on which firms originally procured AI tools.
pts.d: At 44:22–44:58, Williams independently illustrates this issue with Harvey's internet-searching deep research capability. His point is that a tool purchased as a closed environment can acquire outward-facing functionality. The transcript does not demonstrate an actual data leak or contractual breach.

pts.k: Moon regards client-directed AI tooling as an extension of existing client control over working arrangements.
pts.d: At 46:39, Moon responds to Williams's account of practitioners describing institutional clients' tool requirements. She characterises client control over portals and workflows as longstanding, with AI taking it to a new level. Williams's classroom account is second-hand evidence, not an independently measured market-wide purchasing trend.

pts.k: Moon predicts continued AI change will require different working relationships and more communication, collaboration and transparency.
pts.d: At 47:01–49:49, Moon argues that increasingly integrated technology and rapid feature changes will force reconsideration of established practices. She does not accept that simply pointing to existing ethics rules resolves all implementation questions. She presents better systems as an opportunity requiring deliberate choices, rather than an automatic benefit of AI.

pts.k: Williams says improved access to legal AI products has made training more concrete and practice-relevant.
pts.d: At 50:38–52:58, Williams contrasts early teaching that relied heavily on theory and general ChatGPT with more recent access to the tools students will encounter in firms. He credits both vendor availability and an experienced institutional team with supporting safe experimentation and more systematic intake, deployment, measurement and iteration. No learning-outcome statistics are supplied.

pts.k: Moon and Williams distinguish AI-enabled prototyping and learning from the harder work of sustaining deployed legal products.
pts.d: At 54:03–59:49, Moon says building, deployment and maintenance are difficult and that Vanderbilt's principal role is learning and teaching, with partnerships for other builds. Williams describes building as a way for law, data-science and computer-science students to develop a common language, and says generative AI lowers technical access barriers. Their Tennessee end-of-life planning tool illustrates the gap between making a prototype and maintaining a robust service. Moon also describes a planned curated AI-learning repository; this is a project intention, not an established outcome.

pts.k: Williams argues that AI commoditises junior foundational work, disrupting the profession's apprenticeship model.
pts.d: At 1:06:59–1:09:45, Williams says work historically done by first- and second-year associates is increasingly commoditised, raising unresolved questions about how students acquire foundational skills. He combines this with earlier career-choice pressures and possible changes to ownership and firm models, including AI-first firms. He offers no employment series, displacement estimate or evidence that AI alone causes ownership reform. His positive observations about students protecting their learning are explicitly limited to self-selecting upper-year AI students.

pts.k: Moon presents collaboratively redesigned, continually iterative legal education as a desired future.
pts.d: At 1:04:51–1:06:58, Moon expressly frames her answer as the future she wants, not a settled forecast. As firms reconsider what they need from human lawyers, she sees an opportunity for educators, practitioners and students to co-create training rather than operate in separate camps. She expects iteration to extend to legal education but does not specify the resulting curriculum or professional role.

pts.k: Moon acknowledges indications of slower AI uptake among women but questions an epidemic framing and emphasises demonstrated engagement.
pts.d: At 24:46–32:47, Moon draws on participation in cross-disciplinary events to describe women's interest in AI. She acknowledges unspecified uptake studies but does not regard the evidence as strong enough to establish an epidemic. Predictions about widening employment and pay gaps are positions she reports from other research or commentary, not findings established or independently endorsed here. Her own argument is that the narrative matters and should be reshaped.

pts.k: Williams describes AI governance as interdisciplinary and data-centre energy politics as moving into mainstream electoral debate.
pts.d: At 01:58–09:49, Williams says applied legal AI leads directly into organisational responsibility, regulation and compliance, while governance means different things to different stakeholders. He describes data-centre politics as becoming salient between symposium planning and delivery, and predicts attention around the coming midterms. This is an adjacent AI-governance claim, supported by symposium experience and a classroom news example, not a quantified prediction of legal-market growth or election results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source primarily offers first-hand teaching, product and advisory experience, supplemented by second-hand examples and unspecified research.
pts.d: Williams relies on student reports, work with smaller firms, vendor agreements, changing product functionality and VAILL projects. Moon relies on teaching, institutional experimentation and convening experience. ISO 42001 supplies a referenced governance standard, not a performance test. Women's uptake studies are not identified or quantified. Practitioner descriptions of client requirements are second-hand. There are no model benchmarks, measured legal-service productivity effects, systematic learning comparisons or labour-market estimates supporting the broad forecasts. Host-only examples and statistics are not treated as the interviewees' claims.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most observations concern recent changes; longer-term claims remain conditional, exploratory or aspirational.
pts.d: Relative to the episode labelled 2026, Williams compares student exposure over the previous two years, tool access over the previous year, and procurement-standard maturity over the previous eight to twelve months. These relative periods should not be converted into precise calendar dates without a recording date. Moon's organisational-change forecast assumes continued integration and rapid technological change. The closing education discussion is prompted by a next-few-years horizon, but neither guest provides a firm implementation schedule. Williams qualifies student observations through self-selection; Moon explicitly labels educational redesign as a desired future and allows courses without AI integration.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects vary across firm resources, educational roles, client power and participation in AI.
pts.d: Boutique and mid-sized firms face constrained procurement capacity; larger firms generally have more established processes. Firms and in-house teams must address changing tools and governance responsibilities. Institutional clients can influence workflows, with Moon treating this as an extension of existing relationships. Law students and junior associates face changing skill-formation pathways, while educators and law-school labs must rethink training and sustainable product development. Women across disciplines are affected by uptake narratives and opportunities to participate. Data-centre communities and policymakers face energy and electoral issues. The access-to-justice example concerns a lab's product-development limits, not demonstrated closure of the justice gap.
